# Q fever

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Zoonoses and vector-borne diseases > Q fever*

[Original Article Link](/library/lH0vqh)

---

## Summary

Q <u>fever</u> is a notifiable <u>zoonotic disease</u> caused by <u>Coxiella burnetii</u>. Infection can occur directly (without a <u>vector</u>) or via <u>vector</u> transmission (e.g., inhalation of aerosols). There are 2 types of Q <u>fever</u>, acute and <u>chronic Q fever</u>. <u>Acute Q fever</u> occurs 2–6 weeks after infection and manifests mainly with <u>flu-like symptoms</u> and possibly <u>atypical pneumonia</u> and/or <u>hepatitis</u>. <u>Chronic Q fever</u> occurs months to years after infection and manifests with low-grade <u>fever</u> and often <u>endocarditis</u>. The best initial test for both, acute and <u>chronic Q fever</u>, is <u>indirect fluorescent antibody test</u> (<u>IFA</u>). Treatment for <u>acute Q fever</u> includes <u>doxycycline</u> and for <u>chronic Q fever</u> <u>doxycycline</u> PLUS <u>hydroxychloroquine</u>.

---

## Etiology

### <u>Pathogen</u>



* <u>Coxiella burnetii</u> (gram-negative, intracellular)

* Morphological similarities to <u>Rickettsia</u>

* Can survive in harsh environments in a spore-like form




### Route of transmission




* Direct infection (no <u>vector</u> transmission)

* <u>Vector</u> transmission: primary reservoir are cattle, sheep, and goats 

* Inhalation of spore-containing aerosols from the <u>amniotic fluid</u> or secretions of infected livestock

* Ingestion of raw milk produced by infected animals





### Risk groups



* Slaughterhouse workers, farmers, shepherds, veterinarians

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Acute Q fever | <br>Chronic Q fever<br> |
| <br><u>Incubation period</u> [[3]](/library/DRX16B) |  | <br>* 2–6 weeks<br><br> | <br>* Months to years<br><br> |
| Clinical features |  | <br><br>* Often asymptomatic.<br><br>* <u>Flu-like symptoms</u>, which last for 1–2 weeks<br><br>* High-grade <u>fever</u>, chills, <u>malaise</u>, <u>myalgia</u><br><br>* <u>Headache</u>, retroorbital <u>pain</u>, <u>photophobia</u><br><br>* <u>Rhinitis</u>, <u>pharyngitis</u>, <u>laryngitis</u><br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>diarrhea</u><br><br>* <u>Atypical pneumonia</u>: generally mild with nonproductive <u>cough</u> and <u>fever</u><br><br>* <u>Hepatitis</u>, possibly<br><br>* <u>hepatomegaly</u> without <u>jaundice</u><br><br>* Rare manifestations<br><br>* <u>Meningoencephalitis</u><br><br>* <u>Acute endocarditis</u> associated with <u>antiphospholipid syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Immunosuppression</u><br><br>* Post-Q fever fatigue syndrome: one of the most frequent sequelae of <u>acute Q fever</u><br><br>* Fatigue, <u>headache</u><br><br>* Night sweats<br><br>* <u>Arthralgia</u>, <u>myalgia</u>, <u>fasciculations</u><br><br>* Blurred <u>vision</u><br><br>* Painful <u>lymphadenopathy</u><br><br>* <u>Pregnancy</u>: ↑ risk of <u>spontaneous abortion</u>, <u>intrauterine growth retardation</u>, <u>intrauterine fetal death</u>, and <u>premature delivery</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Low-grade <u>fever</u><br><br>* Night sweats, fatigue<br><br>* Weight loss<br><br>* Swelling arms/legs<br><br>* <u>Endocarditis</u>: chronic Q-<u>fever</u> is the most common cause of culture-negative <u>endocarditis</u>.<br><br>* Culture-negative <u>osteomyelitis</u><br><br><br> |
| Diagnostics | <u>Serology</u> via <u>IFA</u> (best initial test) | <br><br>* Anti-phase II <u>antibody</u> <u>IgG</u> <u>titers</u> ≥ 200 and <u>IgM</u> <u>titers</u> ≥ 50<br><br>* <u>IgM antibodies</u> against phase II <u>antigens</u> > <u>antibodies</u> against phase I <u>antigens</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Anti-phase I <u>antibody</u> <u>IgG</u> <u>titers</u> > 800 or persistently high levels of anti-phase I <u>antibodies</u> 6 months after completing therapy<br><br>* <u>Antibodies</u> against phase I <u>antigens</u> > <u>antibodies</u> against phase II <u>antigens</u><br><br><br> |
| Additional findings | <br><br>* If <u>IFA</u> is negative, perform <u>PCR</u> of serum or tissue samples.<br><br>* <u>Blood cultures</u> are often negative.<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br><br>* ↑ <u>Liver</u> enzymes<br><br>* <u>Leukocytosis</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u><br><br>* Chest <u>x-ray</u>: round opacities in patients with <u>atypical pneumonia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Echocardiography</u>: often nonspecific<br><br>* <u>Duke criteria</u> can be used to diagnose <u>endocarditis</u>.<br><br><br> |  |  |
| Treatment |  | <br><br>* First-line: <u>doxycycline</u> for 2 weeks<br><br>* Second-line: <u>macrolides</u> (e.g., <u>azithromycin</u>)<br><br>* Among pregnant women or children < 8 years with mild disease: <u>trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* First-line: <u>doxycycline</u> PLUS <u>hydroxychloroquine</u> for ≥ 18 months<br><br>* Second-line: <u>rifampin</u> PLUS <u>doxycycline</u>/<u>ciprofloxacin</u><br><br>* <u>Valve repair</u> may be required in the case of <u>endocarditis</u>.<br><br><br> |

## Prevention

* Avoid consumption of unpasteurized milk products
